parsed.explanation: No visitor-facing legal restriction is documented: no criminalisation of gender expression, no border or document rules touching trans visitors, no facility bans, and decriminalisation is settled with no reversal. The dominant documented exposure is consequence-after-discovery: trans people face assault at a reported rate several times background, and police dismiss complaints based on identity-card markers, producing documented impunity — a tier-3 societal-hostility pattern with thin recourse, not state targeting. Healthcare discrimination is documented but partially offset by a 2021 medical-council code and a 2020 GBV-care SOP requiring gender-identity-sensitive service. Institutional climate is improving (2024 judiciary/cabinet training, first parliamentary dialogue). Social invisibility rather than open persecution lowers everyday exposure. This sits above tier-3-heavy dossiers with state hostility but clearly below protection-functioning jurisdictions.

entry_documents.exposure: Not documented. No border, visa, or scanner friction for trans visitors is recorded; the marker-change pathway concerns residents only.
entry_documents.interaction: Visitor documents are home-issued; domestic LGR absence does not touch the traveller.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Not documented as visitor-facing. Police dismissal of trans victims' complaints is documented but as refusal of protection, not detention. No custody-placement rules recorded.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: A visitor reporting assault risks the documented dismissal pattern (complaint read by card marker).

federal_state_facilities.exposure: Not documented. No facility or bathroom restrictions recorded.

care_services.exposure: Discrimination in healthcare access singled out: trans people turned away or poorly served (documented, resident-skewed).
care_services.protection: 2021 medical-council code of professional fidelity; 2020 GBV SOP requires gender-identity-sensitive care with tailored case management — paper protections not shown operating.
care_services.interaction: A visitor needing care may face refusal; SOP offers a textual claim but no demonstrated remedy.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: Police dismiss anti-trans violence, framing it by card marker; families pressure victims to accept it; practical impunity documented (Nov 2024).
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: None operative; LGBTIQ-committee referrals are slow.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: No criminal statute targets trans people; enforcement failure, not hostile law, is the operative regime.

minors_guardians.exposure: Resident-facing only (school dropout, youth registration counts); nothing reaching travelling minors.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: Reported assault rate for trans people over four times general population (survey basis unverified); historic pattern is invisibility and little violence (2015), so currency uncertain.
street_violence_police_response.protection: Police response documented as dismissive; impunity is the operative outcome.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Visitor as soft target for robbery/non-reporting is an open question, not documented.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: No anti-discrimination law; no recourse shown to work for trans victims; no relationship recognition for a partner read as same-sex.
remedies_unknowns.protection: 2024 judiciary/cabinet training and first parliamentary dialogue signal institutional improvement, not yet remedy.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Unresolved which marker-change pathway operates (resident-facing); thin but improving institutional climate.

anchor_checks.comparison: Both feature healthcare friction and partial institutional improvisation, but 0.55-C's worst harm is ward placement by marker with advocates available; here the worst documented harm is violence with police impunity — slightly worse recourse, slightly worse severity, offset by no universal-exposure measures.

0.35-B involves police actively targeting trans visitors with stops, confiscation and files. Here police are passive and dismissive rather than predatory, no visitor-directed enforcement exists, and society is invisible-tolerant rather than hostile — materially above that anchor.

0.75-D has equality law, hate-crime recourse and perpetrators prosecuted when caught. Here no protections exist and police decline trans complaints, so victims lack the remedy 0.75-D offers — clearly below it, though both share street-violence as the main risk.

parsed.synthesis: The combined operative regime presents no visitor-facing legal restriction at any journey stage: entry, documents, facilities and custody are unexposed on the record. The exposure concentrates after social discovery — an assault risk reported well above background, met by documented police dismissal and impunity, plus healthcare access discrimination only partially checked by untested professional standards. Recourse is thin; institutions show an improving climate (2024 judicial and executive training, first parliamentary dialogue) but no demonstrated functioning remedy. Social pattern is invisibility and family pressure rather than organised or state targeting. This places the jurisdiction between the tier-3 societal-hostility band and the partial-protection band: safer than any state-directed-targeting or universal-exposure regime, materially riskier than jurisdictions where courts and police demonstrably work for trans people.
